item.title: Fused Message Passing on Apple Silicon
item.dc:creator: Vinay Pandya
item.description:
NoteTL;DR
  • GNN layers in mlx-graphs used to copy a feature row for every edge and then scatter them back. We fused that into one sparse matrix multiply (SpMM) kernel in mlx-cluster, with a full backward pass.
  • Two layouts: COO (one thread per edge, atomics) and CSR (one thread per destination row, no atomics, deterministic).
  • On an M4 Pro, CSR runs a 1M-edge layer about 2–8× faster than the old path and uses up to 15× less memory.
  • On an M1 with a power-law graph, CSR is up to 93× faster. The reason is that it never needs a floating-point atomic, and on the M1 those get very slow when many threads hit the same “hub” node.
  • The same lesson fixed one last slow spot: node degrees are now counted with integer atomics instead of float ones.

1 The problem: one copy per edge

Almost every GNN layer does the same thing. For each node, look at its neighbours, take their features (maybe scaled by an edge weight), and combine them with a sum, mean, max or min. In mlx-graphs this was written in the most direct way possible:

msgs = x[src]                 # gather:  [E, D] — one row per edge
msgs = msgs * w[:, None]      # multiply (optional edge weight)
out  = scatter_add(msgs, dst) # scatter: [N, D]

It’s easy to read, but the middle array has one row for every edge, not every node. A graph with 1M edges and 64 features makes a 256 MB temporary, and autograd keeps a few more of those around for the backward pass. All of it is written to memory and then read back once.

There’s a better way. The three steps together are just a sparse matrix times a dense matrix, out = A @ X, where A is the adjacency matrix. A dedicated kernel can read each neighbour’s row and add it straight into the output, so the [E, D] array never exists.

The fused kernel never materialises anything of size E×D. The only extra memory is the index arrays, which you already have.

2 Two ways to store a graph: COO and CSR

A common reference point is PyG’s CUDA implementation (torch_sparse), which works with the COO format. COO and CSR are just two ways to write down the same edges.

COO (coordinate) is two parallel lists, row and col, one entry per edge. It’s what edge_index already is. CSR (compressed sparse row) sorts edges by destination and replaces the row list with a short rowptr array: node i’s neighbours live at col[rowptr[i] : rowptr[i+1]].

Same 8 directed edges (each undirected edge stored both ways). In CSR, destination 2's neighbours are the contiguous slice col[4:7], so one thread can own that whole row.

The format decides how you parallelise the GPU work, and that turned out to be the most important choice in the whole project:

  • COO kernel: one thread per edge. Each thread reads x[src] and adds it into out[dst]. Many edges share a dst, so those adds have to be atomic.
  • CSR kernel: one thread (group) per destination row. It loops over that row’s neighbours, sums in registers, and writes out[i] exactly once. No other thread touches that row, so no atomics are needed and the result is the same every run.

3 The kernels, and why we had to write a backward pass

MLX lets an extension define a Primitive: a class with a CPU implementation, a Metal (GPU) implementation, and the derivative rules. We built one SpMM primitive in mlx-cluster that covers both layouts, optional edge weights, and sum/mean/max/min.

Training needs gradients, and MLX can’t differentiate through a hand-written kernel on its own. So we wrote the rules ourselves:

  • Gradient for X: if out = A @ X then dX = Aᵀ @ dOut. That’s another SpMM, just with the edges reversed.
  • Gradient for edge weights: dw[e] = dot(dOut[dst], X[src]), one dot product per edge. This is called SDDMM, and it got its own small kernel.

On the mlx-graphs side, a @fused_message_passing decorator lets a layer opt in. When the layer’s message is the standard “neighbour features × optional weight” pattern, propagate() skips gather/scatter and calls the kernel. Anything else (attention softmax, GINE’s edge MLP) falls back to the old path automatically. GCN, SAGE, GIN and SimpleConv are decorated today.

4 What the GPU trace says

Benchmarks tell you how much faster something is. A GPU trace tells you why. We recorded Metal GPU traces in Xcode of the same work on all three paths: GCNConv on powerlaw-1m with 64 features, two training steps (forward and backward), on an Apple M4 Pro. These traces use the final kernels, including the two CSR improvements described in the next sections.

Old path (gather) COO kernel CSR kernel
GPU time 28.97 ms 4.97 ms (5.8× less) 3.92 ms (7.4× less)
GPU memory 642.86 MiB 186.64 MiB (3.4× less) 251.03 MiB (2.6× less)
Command buffers 14 2 2
Compute encoders 13 1 1
Dispatch calls 32 20 20

4.1 Where the old path’s time goes

On the old path, four kernels take 96% of the GPU time: the scatter-add (36.2%), the multiply by edge weights (34.8%) and two gathers (14.7% and 10.3%). These are exactly the kernels that create, scale and sum up the [E, D] per-edge arrays. The layer’s actual matrix multiply (steel_gemm, the linear projection) takes 0.9%.

Each of those kernels does almost no arithmetic: one multiply or one add per number it reads and writes. Xcode’s counters agree. Per encoder, instruction throughput utilisation stays between about 3% and 23%, so the compute units spend most of their time waiting for data. The work is limited by memory traffic, so the way to speed it up is to move fewer bytes, not to compute faster. That’s exactly what fusing does.

Two more details stand out:

  • 13 encoders down to 1. Because the old path moves hundreds of megabytes per step, MLX splits its work into many separate batches, with idle gaps in between. The fused paths fit both training steps into a single encoder.
  • CSR uses more memory than COO (251 vs. 187 MiB). CSR keeps extra index arrays: the sorted copy of the graph, its transpose for the backward pass, and the long-row chunk tables. It still uses 2.6× less memory than the old path.

4.2 A profiling lesson

Our first CSR traces were misleading. They showed only the COO kernel, and CSR looked no better than COO. Two things combined. Our capture script asked MLX for the gradient alone (mx.grad), and for that loss MLX could skip the forward pass entirely, so the forward CSR kernel never ran. And at that point, CSR’s backward pass still used the COO kernel. Switching the capture to mx.value_and_grad, which forces both passes, fixed the first problem. The next two sections fix CSR itself.

5 The power-law surprise

Real graphs aren’t uniform. Citation networks, social graphs and the web follow a power law: most nodes have a handful of neighbours, and a few “hubs” have an enormous number. Our synthetic powerlaw-1m benchmark graph has exactly that shape: its busiest node has about 134,000 incoming edges.

The naive CSR kernel assigns one thread per row. A GPU kernel only finishes when its slowest thread finishes. So while almost every thread finishes after a few neighbours, the hub’s thread walks through its 134,000 neighbours one by one, and the whole kernel waits for it.

Each bar is one thread's work (schematic). Without chunking, the hub row (red) sets the runtime for the whole kernel. With chunking, the hub is split into 2048-edge pieces that run in parallel, then a small second kernel adds the pieces up in a fixed order.

5.1 The fix: split long rows

When the CSR structure is built (once, then cached), we find every row with more than 256 neighbours and cut it into chunks of 2048 edges. Short rows still use the simple one-thread-per-row kernel. Long rows go through two extra kernels: a partial kernel where each chunk sums its piece in parallel, and a reduce kernel that adds the chunk results in a fixed order. For the biggest hub in powerlaw-1m, that’s about 66 chunks working at once instead of one thread doing all 134,000 edges.

There’s an accuracy bonus too. Adding 134,000 floats one after another builds up rounding error, because each new value is added to an ever-larger running total. Summing 2048 at a time and then combining the totals keeps those errors smaller.

6 A deterministic backward pass

The backward pass needs Aᵀ @ dOut. At first we ran it with the COO kernel and swapped indices, which put the atomics back. So we also build a transposed CSR (edges grouped by source instead of destination), with its own long-row chunks. Now the backward is also one-thread-per-row, atomic-free and gives the same answer every run.

The API stays flexible: you can still call the COO path at any time (no preprocessing needed), and CSR is an option that pays a one-time build cost which the decorator caches per graph.

7 Max and min without storing an argmax

Sum is easy. Max and min needed two tricks.

Forward (COO): Metal has no atomic float max. It does have atomic integer max. We use a standard bit trick that maps each float to an unsigned integer whose ordering matches the float ordering (flip the sign bit for positives, flip all the bits for negatives). Then atomic_fetch_max on the integers gives the float max, and a small decode kernel turns them back into floats.

Backward: the gradient flows only to the neighbour that “won” the max. Instead of saving an argmax array during the forward pass, the backward kernel recomputes it: for each edge, check whether x[src] == out[dst]. Ties get the full gradient, which matches what MLX’s own scatter-max does, and empty rows output 0.

That integer-atomic detail matters for the M1 story below.

8 Results on an M4 Pro

Every number below is forward + backward (value_and_grad), median time, on the synthetic power-law graph with 1M edges and 256 features. GAT is included as a control: its attention softmax isn’t fusable, so all three modes should match, and they do.

M4 Pro, powerlaw-1m, D=256. Lower is better.
Peak memory during forward + backward, same graph. Max and min benefit most because the old path also kept a large argmax buffer.

Two things stand out. First, CSR beats COO even on the M4 Pro, by about 1.5–2× on the plain aggregations. Second, the memory savings are large and they hold for COO and CSR alike, because both remove the [E, D] arrays. On tiny graphs like Cora, the difference is just a fraction of a millisecond either way, since per-call overhead dominates there.

9 Results on an 8 GB M1, and why CSR loves power laws

Then we ran the same benchmark on an M1 MacBook with 8 GB, and the gap got much bigger.

93×CSR vs old path, mean aggregation, powerlaw-1m D=16
48×SAGEConv with CSR, same graph
~1×COO sum vs old path on the same graph. Float atomics are the bottleneck
15×less peak memory for max/min
M1 (8 GB), powerlaw-1m, D=16, forward + backward, measured before the integer degree fix described in the last section. Note how COO sum barely beats the old path while COO max (integer atomics) is already fast.

9.1 So why is CSR so good on power-law graphs?

Take the busiest node in powerlaw-1m, with about 134,000 incoming edges. With 16 features, that means about 2.1 million additions that all land in the same 16 output slots.

Left: thousands of threads issue an atomic float add to the same address, and the hardware handles them one at a time. Right: each chunk adds in its own registers, and only a handful of partial sums meet at the end, in a fixed order.

Here is what each path does with that hub:

  • Old path (gather + scatter_add): MLX’s scatter uses a float atomic add per element. All of those adds target the same 16 addresses, so they queue up. On top of that it moves the full [E, D] array through memory.
  • COO kernel: it removes the big array, but it still issues one float atomic per edge per feature into the hub’s row. The queue is just as long. That’s why COO sum on the M1 is about 72 ms against 77 ms for the old path: it fixed the memory traffic but not the bottleneck.
  • CSR kernel: no atomics at all. The hub’s 134,000 edges are split into about 66 chunks of 2048. Each chunk sums into registers that no other thread can see, and a tiny reduce kernel adds the 66 partial results. There is no queue: 2.3 ms.
TipThe clue that proves it

On the M1, COO max takes 5 ms while COO sum takes 72 ms on the same graph. Both use one atomic per edge into the same hub. The only difference is that max uses integer atomics (thanks to the bit trick) and sum uses float atomics. Contended integer atomics are fine on the M1. Contended float atomics are the problem.

9.2 Why the M4 Pro hides this

Newer Apple GPUs handle contended float atomics much better and have more memory bandwidth, so on the M4 Pro COO only trails CSR by about 2×. The M1 shows the worst case, and its 8 GB of unified memory makes the old path’s big temporary arrays hurt more too. On uniform graphs (no hubs) the M1 gap shrinks back to roughly 2–5×. So the power-law gap is mostly about contention, not raw speed.

Mean aggregation was the most extreme case (93×) because both the old path and COO computed the node degree with another float scatter, which also piled onto the hub. CSR gets degrees for free: rowptr[i+1] - rowptr[i]. That observation led to the last fix in this release.

10 Accuracy and training

Relative error against the old path stays around 10⁻⁷ to 10⁻⁵ in float32, and max/min match exactly. To make the tests fair, we compare against a float64 reference with a tolerance that scales with the magnitude of the result. A hub that sums 134,000 values will always carry some rounding error, in any implementation. The benchmark folder also has train_compare.py, which trains the same model with both paths so you can compare loss curves side by side.

11 Counting degrees with integers

The M1 results pointed at one more float-atomic hotspot outside our kernels: counting each node’s neighbours. Mean aggregation divides a sum by that count, and GCN normalisation uses it too. Both counted by scatter-adding 1.0 per edge, so on powerlaw-1m about 134,000 float atomic adds queued on the hub’s single counter. That’s why COO mean sat at about 253 ms on the M1 (against 72 ms for COO sum), and why GCNConv was still about 180 ms even with CSR.

The fix, in this release, is to count with an int32 scatter and convert to float32 afterwards:

deg = mx.zeros((num_nodes,), dtype=mx.int32).at[index].add(1).astype(mx.float32)
  • In mlx-cluster, spmm_coo(reduce="mean") counts this way. spmm_csr doesn’t need it, because it reads degrees from rowptr.
  • In mlx-graphs, degree() counts this way whenever no edge weights are given. That speeds up every caller: mean aggregation on the gather-scatter path, scatter_max / scatter_min (which use it to find nodes with no neighbours) and unweighted GCNConv.
  • Nothing else changes. Counts are whole numbers, so the int32 result is exact, and the output is still float32. int32 rather than int64, because MLX’s GPU scatter doesn’t support int64. Converting back to float is one pass over the nodes with no contention, so it costs a fraction of a millisecond.
  • Weighted degrees (a sum of edge weights) still use float atomics, since the weights aren’t whole numbers.

Numbers come from benchmarks/spmm/bench_fused_mp.py in mlx-graphs, run with MLX 0.32.4 on an Apple M4 Pro and an Apple M1 (8 GB). Kernels live in mlx_cluster/sparse/. Documentation: fused message passing in mlx-graphs.

item.title: Scaling ScholarSearch: 15K Papers, Seven Retrievers, One Command on AWS
item.dc:creator: Vinay Pandya
item.description:
Introduction

In the first ScholarSearch post I compared seven retrieval methods over 194 malware-classification papers and 40 queries. It was a good weekend project, but it had two problems: the corpus was too small for the numbers to mean much, and every result came from a pile of one-off scripts that I couldn’t rerun with confidence.

This post is about fixing both. The corpus is now 15,000 papers, the eval set is 100 queries, and every experiment runs from one command that launches a throwaway EC2 instance, writes results to S3 under a run ID, and terminates itself.

Code: github.com/vinayhpandya/search-algorithms

NoteTL;DR
  • HNSW costs essentially nothing in relevance. Swapping exact dense search for HNSW made dense retrieval 25× faster (13.7 → 0.54 ms) and moved NDCG@10 by −0.003.
  • Reranking is the biggest win available. Reranking hybrid’s top 100 lifted NDCG@10 from 0.695 to 0.855 (cross-encoder) and 0.841 (ColBERT).
  • ColBERT is the practical choice. It reached 98% of the cross-encoder’s NDCG@10 at 111 ms vs 6.4 s per query on CPU, provided its document embeddings are precomputed.
  • That precomputation is the real cost: 0.74 s per paper on a 2-vCPU box.
  • BM25 beats dense SPECTER2 by a wide margin on this corpus (0.713 vs 0.528), and part of that is probably a data problem, not a model problem.
  • Judging 698 new query–paper pairs cost $0.05.

What changed since the first post

First post This post
Corpus 194 arXiv papers 15,000 OpenAlex papers ("malware detection"), frozen
Queries 40 100
Relevance labels researcher + critic LLM, human spot-check gpt-4o-mini, graded 0/1/2, pooled: 2,785 labels
Dense model SPECTER2 SPECTER2 (proximity adapter for papers, ad-hoc query adapter for queries)
Where it runs my laptop, many scripts one runner, one EC2 instance, results in S3

The labels are pooled: only papers that some method ranks in its top 10 for a query get judged. That keeps costs tiny, but it has a consequence I’ll come back to in Why the baseline numbers moved.

The pipeline

I spent a while going back and forth on how much infrastructure this needed (Step Functions? AWS Batch? a scheduler?). What I needed was much simpler: one command that reruns everything and leaves a traceable record. So the design is deliberately boring.

A few choices that turned out to matter:

  • Plain EC2, not Batch or Step Functions. The existing Terraform already had a locked-down worker pattern: no inbound ports, an IAM role that can only touch one S3 prefix, SSM for shell access, and a watchdog timer. A new run is a new JSON config, not new infrastructure. The instance terminates rather than stops when the job ends, so a forgotten instance can’t keep billing.
  • Every run gets a folder. runs/<timestamp>-<config>-<hash>/ holds retrieval.json, judge.json, report.json, and a run_manifest.json with the exact config, git commit, per-stage status and timing. Any number in this post traces back to a run.
  • The report refuses to guess. If a method surfaces a paper nobody has judged, the report stage outputs how many pairs are missing instead of an NDCG score. Treating unjudged papers as irrelevant quietly penalizes exactly the methods that find new things.
  • Judging is capped and incremental. The judge stage reuses every existing label, judges only the missing pairs, and keeps a cumulative spend ledger in S3. It stops before a hard cap ($25) would be exceeded. This run used $0.05 of it.
  • The API key never touches disk. It lives in SSM Parameter Store as a SecureString; the worker role can read that one parameter and nothing else.

Results

All seven methods, same 100 queries, same labels. Latency is per-query p50 on an m7i-flex.large (2 vCPUs, CPU only).

Method NDCG@10 MRR@10 (label = 2) p50 latency
BM25 0.713 0.713 32 ms
Dense (exact SPECTER2) 0.528 0.592 13.7 ms
Dense (HNSW) 0.524 0.587 0.54 ms
Hybrid (RRF: BM25 + dense) 0.695 0.746 46 ms
Hybrid (RRF: BM25 + HNSW) 0.696 0.752 33 ms
Hybrid → cross-encoder rerank (top 100) 0.855 0.885 6,389 ms
Hybrid → ColBERT rerank (top 100) 0.841 0.847 111 ms

HNSW is effectively free

Exact dense search scores all 15K vectors per query; HNSW (M=16, efSearch=64) walks a graph instead. That made dense retrieval 25× faster with an NDCG@10 change of −0.003, and the HNSW hybrid is marginally better than the exact one (0.696 vs 0.695), which is noise.

The interesting part is how this squares with the ANN benchmark. In an earlier benchmark on the same vectors, HNSW at this setting returned 96.4% of the exact top-10 neighbours (Recall@10). Missing 3.6% of the nearest vectors translated into almost no loss of relevant papers, because the neighbours HNSW misses are the borderline ones near the cut-off, which are rarely the papers a judge rates highest. ANN recall is a proxy; end-to-end relevance is what users feel, and here the proxy is pessimistic.

At 15K vectors, though, exact search is already fast. The latency win matters at the next scale step, not this one. Hybrid latency is now dominated by BM25 (32 of 33 ms), which is a pure-Python implementation; moving it to a real inverted index is the obvious next speed-up.

Rerankers: the biggest jump in the whole project

Both rerankers take hybrid’s top 100 and reorder them. Both add about 0.15 NDCG@10 on top of the best first-stage method, by far the largest single improvement anywhere in this project.

The difference between them is architecture, and it shows up entirely in latency:

  • A cross-encoder (ms-marco-MiniLM-L-6-v2) reads query and paper together through every transformer layer. Nothing can be precomputed, so every query pays for 100 full forward passes: 6.4 seconds per query on two CPU cores.
  • ColBERT (colbertv2.0) encodes papers and queries separately into one vector per token, then scores with MaxSim: for each query token, take its best-matching paper token, and sum. Paper token embeddings can be computed ahead of time, so at query time you encode one short query and do some matrix multiplies: 111 ms.

ColBERT got 98% of the cross-encoder’s NDCG@10 at 1/58th of the latency. On MRR@10 (label = 2) the gap is a bit larger (0.847 vs 0.885): the cross-encoder is better at putting the single best paper first. With 100 queries and no significance test yet, I wouldn’t read much into a 0.014 NDCG gap; I would read a lot into a 58× latency gap.

This is a different result from the first post, where late interaction trailed the cross-encoder clearly. The setups differ: there ColBERT did full retrieval from a Qdrant multivector index over 194 papers; here it reranks a strong hybrid candidate set over 15K.

ColBERT’s hidden bill

The 111 ms figure assumes paper embeddings already exist. The runner encodes each paper once, caches it, and keeps that work outside the timed region, the way a stored index would behave. That one-off work was not small:

Papers ColBERT had to encode 5,186 (unique papers across 100 queries’ top-100 pools)
Time on 2 vCPUs 3,827 s (64 minutes)
Per paper 0.74 s
Extrapolated: all 15K papers about 3 hours
Extrapolated: 100K papers about 20 hours

That encoding was most of the run’s 1.5 hours. The cross-encoder has no offline cost but pays at every query; ColBERT pays once up front and then is cheap forever. For a corpus that changes slowly, ColBERT’s trade is the better one, but the index build needs a GPU, not two CPU cores.

BM25 vs. dense: probably partly a data problem

The weakest result is dense SPECTER2, 0.19 NDCG@10 below BM25. In the first post they were nearly tied. When I dug into the earlier 15K retrieval results, I found that 38% of dense’s top-10 hits had an empty abstract, versus 17% for BM25. The judge sees only title and abstract, and its rubric rates a paper it can’t assess as not relevant. Papers with only a title still get an embedding, and a plausible explanation is that short title-only embeddings sit close to many queries, so dense keeps retrieving papers the judge can’t credit.

So some of dense’s deficit is the corpus, not the model. That’s the first thing to fix in the next corpus: filter to papers that have abstracts, then see how much of the gap closes.

Hybrid helps the top result, not the whole list

Hybrid is slightly below BM25 on NDCG@10 (0.695 vs 0.713) but above it on MRR@10 (label = 2) (0.746 vs 0.713). With dense this much weaker, fusing it in drags some weaker papers into the top 10, but the papers both methods agree on tend to be the best ones, so the first highly relevant result moves up. Either way, hybrid’s real value here is as a candidate generator for the rerankers.

Why the baseline numbers moved

If you compare this run with my earlier 15K evaluation, BM25 drops from 0.754 to 0.713 and hybrid from 0.731 to 0.695, with the same code, corpus and queries.

That’s pooling at work, not a regression. NDCG divides by the best ranking achievable from the judged papers for each query. The rerankers surfaced 698 query–paper pairs nobody had judged before, many of them relevant, so the ideal ranking got better and every method that didn’t find those papers now scores lower against it. The ordering of the old methods is unchanged. It’s also a good argument for the “refuse to score with unjudged pairs” rule: had those 698 pairs been treated as irrelevant, the rerankers would have been penalized for finding good papers.

Caveats

  • The judge is an LLM. gpt-4o-mini with a fixed 0/1/2 rubric over title and abstract. Unlike the first post, this round had no human spot-check of the labels yet.
  • 100 queries, one run, no confidence intervals. Large gaps (rerankers vs. everything, BM25 vs. dense) are safe; small ones (cross-encoder vs. ColBERT on NDCG) are not.
  • Empty abstracts affect every method, dense the most.
  • CPU-only latency on a small instance. The cross-encoder would be far faster on a GPU, and BM25 is pure Python. Dense latencies exclude query encoding (query vectors are precomputed); reranker latencies include it.
  • Rerankers only reorder what hybrid found. They can’t recover a relevant paper outside hybrid’s top 100.

What it cost

The whole run (installing PyTorch, 100 queries through seven methods, encoding 5,186 papers with ColBERT, and judging 698 new pairs) took about 1.5 hours on a single small CPU instance. The LLM judging cost $0.053. The instance cost was well under a dollar, and it terminated itself when done.

What’s next

  1. Scale to 100K papers with distractors. Keep the 15K security papers and add about 85K papers from other computer-science fields as distractors. They share vocabulary (“detection”, “adversarial”, “graph neural network”) without being relevant, which makes the benchmark harder and more realistic, and is where HNSW and IVF-PQ should actually earn their keep. Filter out papers without abstracts this time.
  2. Store ColBERT token embeddings (≈0.8 GB at 15K, ≈5 GB at 100K in fp16), built on a GPU, then run full ColBERT retrieval in Qdrant instead of reranking only.
  3. A cheaper judge. The 2,785 existing labels are a ready-made answer key for testing a fast classification-style model as a relevance judge: measure agreement first, and adopt it only if method rankings don’t change.
  4. Confidence intervals via paired bootstrap over queries, so the close calls get an honest error bar.

item.title: Fitting a 3B Model on Two GPUs with FSDP: A Practical Walkthrough
item.dc:creator: Vinay Pandya
item.description:
1 Introduction

These are my notes from fine-tuning SmolLM3-3B on a medical Q&A dataset across two GPUs using FSDP (Fully Sharded Data Parallel). The goal was practical: understand what FSDP actually does to memory, why it’s necessary here rather than optional, and what breaks along the way.

The motivating constraint is concrete. A 3B model sounds small — 6 GB of weights in bf16 — so surely it trains on any modern GPU. It doesn’t. On the A100-40GB I was running, the naive full-replica approach doesn’t fit at all. FSDP is what makes this model trainable on that hardware, and understanding why is the whole point.

NoteWhat this post is

The reasoning and the gotchas behind one real FSDP run, using Hugging Face’s Trainer / TRL SFTTrainer where FSDP is configured rather than hand-written. Code lives at the end.

2 Why the model doesn’t fit: where the memory goes

The intuition that trips people up: parameter count barely predicts training memory. The weights are the small part. Everything around them — gradients and, above all, the optimizer state — is what fills the GPU.

For a model with parameters trained with Adam in mixed precision, the static per-GPU cost — present before a single activation — looks like this:

Component Precision Bytes/param For 3B
Weights bf16 2 ~6 GB
Gradients bf16 2 ~6 GB
Adam moment m fp32 4 ~12 GB
Adam variance v fp32 4 ~12 GB
Static total ~12 ~36 GB

Activations sit on top of that (gradient checkpointing keeps them small). So the real number to plan around is ~36–42 GB, not 6 GB.

Code 
def static_memory_gb(params_billion, num_gpus=1, sharded=False):
    """Rough per-GPU static training memory (weights + grads + Adam), mixed precision."""
    P = params_billion * 1e9
    weights = 2 * P      # bf16
    grads   = 2 * P      # bf16
    adam    = 8 * P      # fp32 m + fp32 v
    total_bytes = weights + grads + adam
    if sharded:
        total_bytes /= num_gpus   # FSDP: sharded across ranks
    return total_bytes / 1e9

print(f"full replica, 1 GPU: ~{static_memory_gb(3):.0f} GB")
print(f"FSDP sharded, 2 GPU: ~{static_memory_gb(3, num_gpus=2, sharded=True):.0f} GB")

2.1 Why this rules out a single-GPU full replica

That ~36–42 GB peak lands right on top of a 40 GB card’s ceiling — no room for activations, CUDA context, or NCCL buffers. In practice it OOMs. The table shows how tight it is:

GPU VRAM Full replica (~40 GB peak) FSDP sharded / 2 GPU (~18 GB)
A10G 24 GB ❌ OOM ✅
A100 40 GB 40 GB ❌ OOM / knife-edge ✅
L40S 48 GB ✅ (small headroom) ✅
A100 80 GB 80 GB ✅ comfortable ✅
WarningBatch size is the wrong lever

When you OOM, the reflex is to drop the batch size. But batch size only scales activation memory — the small part, especially with gradient checkpointing on. The ~36 GB of weights + grads + optimizer state doesn’t move. If the static cost doesn’t fit, sharding is the fix, not a smaller batch.

3 What FSDP does about it

FSDP’s core idea: don’t keep a full copy of the model on every GPU. Partition the weights, gradients, and optimizer state across the ranks, and reconstruct each layer’s full weights just in time for the forward and backward pass, then throw them away again.

Concretely, per training step FSDP:

  1. All-gathers each layer’s sharded weights into the full layer, right before it’s needed.
  2. Runs forward / backward on the full layer, then frees the gathered weights.
  3. Reduce-scatters the gradients back down to shards.
  4. Keeps only its shard of the optimizer state.

The result on 2 GPUs: that ~36 GB static cost becomes ~18 GB per GPU. The price is communication — the all-gathers and reduce-scatters are extra traffic every step. That’s the fundamental FSDP trade: communication in exchange for memory. When the model won’t fit otherwise, it’s a trade you happily take, because the alternative is not training at all.

4 Configuring FSDP with the HF Trainer

The relevant switch in SFTConfig / TrainingArguments:

Code 
fsdp_arg = "full_shard auto_wrap"
fsdp_config = {
    # Force FSDP1 (flat params) instead of FSDP2 (DTensor). See gotcha #1 below.
    "fsdp_version": 1,
    # Wrap at the model's actual decoder-layer class -- NOT "LlamaDecoderLayer".
    # Auto-wrap needs the right class name to find shard boundaries.
    "fsdp_transformer_layer_cls_to_wrap": ["SmolLM3DecoderLayer"],
    "fsdp_backward_prefetch": "backward_pre",   # overlap comms with compute
    "fsdp_state_dict_type": "SHARDED_STATE_DICT",
    "fsdp_offload_params": False,               # True if you're still OOMing
}

Two details that matter more than they look:

  1. The wrap class must be exact. For SmolLM3 it’s SmolLM3DecoderLayer, not the Llama name you might copy from a tutorial. Get it wrong and auto-wrap can’t find layer boundaries to shard at — you silently lose most of the memory savings.
  2. fsdp_offload_params=True is your escape hatch if even sharded params don’t fit — it pushes them to CPU RAM at a throughput cost. The last resort before “get a bigger GPU.”

5 The gotchas (this is the useful part)

Getting FSDP configured was easy. Getting a run to actually finish surfaced three failures that no tutorial warned me about. Each looked scary and had a one-line fix.

5.1 Gotcha 1 — FSDP2’s DTensor error after the first eval

The run trained cleanly for ~100 steps, ran a full eval, then died:

RuntimeError: aten.embedding.default: got mixed torch.Tensor and DTensor,
need to convert all torch.Tensor to DTensor before calling distributed operators!

Modern FSDP (FSDP2, fully_shard) represents sharded params as DTensor. Some params — notably tied embeddings — can end up as plain torch.Tensor while the rest are DTensor, and the next forward after an eval/checkpoint cycle mixes the two. It characteristically fires right after the first eval, which is why it ran fine for 100 steps first.

TipFix

Pin FSDP1: "fsdp_version": 1. FSDP1 uses flat parameters, not DTensor, so the mixed-tensor path can’t occur. (Tracked upstream in transformers #42417 and pytorch #153354.)

5.2 Gotcha 2 — checkpoint save fills the disk and truncates

With FSDP1 in place, the run then crashed at the first checkpoint save:

save_fsdp_optimizer → dist_cp.save → torch.save → write_end_of_file()
RuntimeError: [enforce fail at inline_container.cc:626] . unexpected pos 448 vs 342

That unexpected pos from torch’s inline_container is a truncated write — the file write failed partway. The cause: an FSDP checkpoint saves weights plus the full fp32 Adam state (~30 GB+ for 3B), and that overflowed the container’s ephemeral disk on the first save. Ironically, the same optimizer state that forces you to use FSDP is also what blows up the checkpoint.

TipFix

If you only want the final model, stop periodic checkpoints entirely: save_strategy="no". The explicit save_model() + push_to_hub() at the end still run. For crash-resilient long runs, instead mount a large volume at output_dir so there’s real disk to write to.

5.3 Gotcha 3 — metrics logged to the wrong place

Training metrics weren’t showing on the dashboard. The logs revealed two separate experiment-tracker sessions: a manual init() that got closed before training, and the Trainer’s built-in callback — which does its own init() and reads its target from environment variables, defaulting to a local directory inside the container that’s discarded when the job ends.

TipFix

Don’t hand-roll a second tracker session. Set the env vars the callback actually reads (e.g. TRACKIO_PROJECT, TRACKIO_SPACE_ID) before the Trainer starts, and let the single built-in callback own logging.

NoteThe pattern across all three

None of these were FSDP “not working.” They were interactions at the seams — FSDP × eval, FSDP × disk, Trainer × tracker. Distributed training is mostly debugging the seams, and the logs told the exact story every time. Read them top-to-bottom before changing config.

6 Benchmarking the FSDP run

The training script exposes a benchmark mode: cap the run to a fixed number of steps, log every step, skip the model push, and capture a torch.profiler trace.

# FSDP timed run with profiler
TRAIN_STRATEGY=fsdp BENCHMARK_STEPS=10 ENABLE_PROFILER=true \
    modal run --detach launch_on_modal.py --script "launch_command.sh"
Code 
import pandas as pd
import plotly.graph_objects as go
from plotly.subplots import make_subplots

# NOTE: placeholder values. Replace with numbers from your BENCHMARK run
# (trainer metrics: train_samples_per_second, train_steps_per_second; and
# peak per-GPU memory from the profiler trace).
bench = pd.DataFrame({
    "Metric": ["Peak mem / GPU (GB)", "Samples / sec", "Steps / sec"],
    "FSDP":   [None, None, None],
})

fig = go.Figure(go.Bar(x=bench["Metric"], y=bench["FSDP"],
                       marker_color="#27AE60"))
fig.update_layout(height=350, margin=dict(t=40, b=40, l=60, r=40),
                  title_text="FSDP run summary")
fig.show()
WarningHonesty note

The chart above is intentionally empty — I’d rather ship a template than invented numbers. Drop in your own train_samples_per_second and the profiler’s peak-memory figure once the benchmark run completes.

6.1 Reading the profiler trace

Here’s what the actual FSDP trace from this run looks like, loaded in Perfetto:

Reading it top to bottom:

  • thread 231 (python) — the main Python thread dispatching work. The long green blocks are the framework driving the step; the early gap at the far left is warmup settling before the profiler’s active window.
  • thread 289 (pt_autograd_0) — the autograd (backward) thread. Those repeated sawtooth / “tree” shapes are the per-decoder-layer work — one repeated unit per wrapped SmolLM3DecoderLayer. That regular, repeating structure is exactly what you want to see: it means auto-wrap sharded at layer granularity as configured, so each layer is gathered → computed → freed in a tidy cycle.
  • Thread 0 (main thread) — the thin orange tick marks are CUDA kernel launches from the host. They’re evenly spaced, i.e. the CPU is feeding the GPU steadily and isn’t stalling.
  • CUDA stream 7 — the main compute stream. This is where the actual matmuls/attention kernels for the forward and backward pass run.
  • CUDA stream 16 — the NCCL execution stream. Slices here are named things like ncclDevKernel_AllGather_RING_LL(...) with Category: kernel — this is the literal collective communication kernel moving bytes between GPUs.
  • CUDA stream 17 — the FSDP annotation stream. Slices here are named FSDP::all_gather (model.layers.N) with Category: gpu_user_annotation — a profiler-inserted label wrapping the all-gather operation for a specific layer, useful for seeing which layer a given burst of comms belongs to.
  • ProfilerStep#2/#3/#4 label the three steps captured by the schedule (wait=1, warmup=1, active=3). The important read: streams 7, 16 and 17 are near-continuously filled with almost no white gaps — the GPU is busy end to end, and compute overlaps with the communication streams rather than stalling on it. That’s backward_prefetch="backward_pre" doing its job.
TipWhy you’ll see two all-gathers overlapping, not one at a time

Zoom into stream 17 and you’ll often catch two adjacent FSDP::all_gather regions for different layers sitting close together — e.g. model.layers.21 and model.layers.23 back-to-back rather than cleanly sequential. That’s prefetch, not a bug or duplicate work:

  1. While GPU 0 is computing layer 21’s forward/backward pass on stream 7, FSDP simultaneously kicks off the all-gather for layer 23’s weights on streams 16/17, in the background.
  2. Because the all-gather runs on a separate stream, its network communication overlaps with layer 21’s matmuls instead of blocking them.
  3. By the time layer 21’s compute finishes, layer 23’s full weights are already sitting there — so compute can move straight into layer 23 with no wait. Worked example with 2 GPUs and 4 layers, each layer’s weights split in half across the two ranks:
Layer GPU 0 holds GPU 1 holds
1 half of Layer 1 other half
2 half of Layer 2 other half
3 half of Layer 3 other half
4 half of Layer 4 other half

Neither GPU alone has enough of any single layer to compute with — that’s the memory saving. The naive approach (gather → compute → reshard → gather → compute → …, one layer at a time, fully serial) would stall compute on every layer’s network round-trip. Prefetching hides that cost: the all-gather for layer N+1 is issued while layer N is still computing, so by the time layer N finishes, layer N+1’s weights are ready. Over a full step you’ll also see this happen twice per layer — once before forward, once before backward — since FSDP reshards after forward to keep the memory savings, then has to re-gather before backward needs the full weights again.

NoteWhat’s healthy here

The two signals that say this run is compute-bound, not communication-bound: (1) the CUDA streams have very little idle white space, and (2) the per-layer sawtooth in the autograd thread is regular — no long flat stretches where a rank is waiting on an all-gather. On 2 GPUs with layer-wrapped FSDP and prefetch on, that’s the outcome you’re aiming for.

WarningWhere the bottleneck would show up

This zoomed-out view can hide things a kernel-level zoom would reveal. To confirm communication isn’t the limiter, zoom into a single ProfilerStep and look for:

  • Gaps on stream 7 (compute) that line up with active ncclDevKernel_AllGather slices on stream 16 → comms not overlapping; try tuning prefetch or limit_all_gathers.
  • stream 25, which fires only in short bursts at the step boundaries here — likely the boundary collective (e.g. gradient reduction / optimizer step). If those bursts grow relative to the step, the sync at the boundary is your cost.
  • The sparse orange band at the very start — warmup/setup, correctly excluded from the active measurement window. For this run, none of those dominate — the story is a well-overlapped, compute-bound FSDP step.

7 Recommendations

  1. Reach for FSDP full_shard when the model + optimizer state won’t fit as a full replica. It divides the static memory by the number of GPUs.
  2. Wrap at the correct decoder-layer class — the single most common way to silently lose the savings.
  3. Turn on fsdp_offload_params=True if sharding alone isn’t enough. It trades speed for headroom.
  4. Pin fsdp_version: 1 until the FSDP2/DTensor + eval interaction is resolved in your stack.

8 Lessons learned

NoteKey takeaways
  1. Parameter count lies about training memory. A 3B model needs ~36 GB of static state under Adam. Plan for weights + grads + 2× fp32 optimizer state, not just weights.
  2. FSDP trades communication for memory. That’s the whole deal — it shards the state so a model that can’t fit as a replica becomes trainable.
  3. Sharding, not batch size, is the memory lever. Batch size only touches activations.
  4. The failures are at the seams. FSDP × eval, FSDP × disk, Trainer × tracker. Read the traceback fully; each of mine had a one-line fix.
  5. A bigger GPU isn’t always more memory. A100-40GB < L40S-48GB. Check the actual VRAM, not the model name.

9 Appendix: reproduction

Code, launch scripts, and configuration:

https://github.com/vinayhpandya/distributed_machine_learning_practice

# FSDP fine-tune, detached so it survives a closed terminal
TRAIN_STRATEGY=fsdp modal run --detach launch_on_modal.py --script "launch_command.sh"

# Follow logs / check status
modal app logs smolm-medical-training

Notes from a distributed-training practice project. Corrections welcome.

item.title: Rediska: Architecture and Performance Notes for a Go-Based Redis Clone
item.dc:creator: Vinay Pandya
item.description:
1 Introduction

Rediska is a Redis clone I’ve been building in Go, mostly as a way to actually understand what Redis does under the hood — RESP parsing, an in-memory store, AOF persistence, transactions, HyperLogLog, pipelining, eviction policies — rather than just using it. This post walks through how it’s put together, what it currently supports, and how it stacks up against real Redis on redis-benchmark.

NoteWhat this post covers
  • The dispatch architecture: connections, a shared command channel, and a single worker
  • What’s implemented so far: persistence, expiry, eviction, transactions, HyperLogLog, pipelining
  • Graceful shutdown, and why it needs more than “just close the socket”
  • How it compares to real Redis on benchmarks, and what the gap is likely coming from
  • What’s left to test to pin that down further

2 Architecture: One Channel, One Worker

Every client connection runs on its own goroutine, reading RESP commands off the socket. None of those goroutines touch the store directly. Instead, every command — plain, pipelined, or part of a transaction — gets wrapped into a request (holding the command itself, or a batch, or a pipeline, plus a reply channel) and dropped into a single shared, buffered channel. Exactly one goroutine, the dispatch worker, ever reads from that channel: it loops for as long as the channel stays open, pulls one request at a time, runs the appropriate command logic, and sends the result back down that request’s own reply channel.

This is deliberate: the store is a plain map with zero locking. As long as exactly one goroutine ever touches it, that’s safe with no mutex required. The trade-off is that every command now has to travel through a channel to reach that goroutine — the connection goroutine sends its request and blocks until the worker sends a reply back, before it can write anything to the socket.

3 What’s Implemented

3.1 Persistence and expiry

Rediska supports an append-only file (AOF) mode: every write command is logged, and on startup the server replays the file to recover state. Keys can carry a TTL, and expiry is handled two ways — lazily, when a read touches an already-expired key, and actively, via a ticking goroutine that periodically sweeps the keyspace for expired entries and removes them (backing off once it stops finding many, the same general pattern real Redis uses).

3.2 Eviction policies

When a maxmemory limit is set, rediska supports both an approximate-LRU policy (sampling a handful of keys and evicting the least-recently-used among them, rather than tracking exact global recency) and an LFU policy with a logarithmic counter and configurable decay, matching the shape of Redis’s own LFU implementation. Memory usage is tracked per-key so eviction decisions have real data to sample from.

3.3 Transactions

MULTI/EXEC/DISCARD are implemented via a small per-connection state machine. Every parsed command while inside a MULTI block is classified as either a normal command to queue (acknowledged with +QUEUED), a transaction-control reply that doesn’t touch the store, or EXEC itself — which sends the whole queued batch through the dispatch channel as one request. The worker runs every command in that batch back-to-back with nothing else able to interleave, and wraps the results into a single RESP array, matching Redis’s atomicity guarantee: a transaction executes as one indivisible block.

3.4 HyperLogLog

Rediska implements PFADD, PFCOUNT, and PFMERGE — a probabilistic cardinality estimator that lets you count approximately how many distinct elements have been added to a key using a fixed, small amount of memory regardless of how many elements go in. It supports both the sparse and dense internal encodings Redis itself uses (sparse for small cardinalities, promoting to dense as a key sees more distinct values), rather than always paying the dense representation’s memory cost upfront.

3.5 Pipelining

A pipelining client fires several commands without waiting for replies between them. After decoding one command, the connection handler checks whether more data is already sitting in the read buffer — meaning it arrived over the network already, no blocking read needed — and if so, keeps decoding into a batch instead of dispatching one command at a time. Once everything currently available is collected, the whole batch ships through the channel as a single request, and the worker concatenates each command’s individual reply into one response — one channel round trip for N commands instead of N.

3.6 Monitoring and graceful shutdown

An INFO command exposes keyspace and server stats in the format a Redis exporter expects, so Prometheus/Grafana can scrape it like real Redis. On shutdown (SIGINT/SIGTERM), the server stops accepting new connections, waits for every in-flight connection and the expiry goroutine to finish (tracked via a sync.WaitGroup), only then closes the dispatch channel, waits for the worker to fully drain it, and finally syncs and closes the AOF file — in that order, since each step depends on the one before it having actually completed, not just been requested.

4 How It Compares to Redis

Benchmarked with redis-benchmark against real Redis on the same machine. The starting point was roughly half of Redis’s throughput and double its latency. After a round of profiling-driven fixes — removing unconditional per-command debug logging, replacing per-command read-deadline syscalls with a single shutdown-watcher goroutine, pooling reply channels instead of allocating one per command, and reducing RESP parsing overhead — single-command (non-pipelined) throughput closed to roughly 1.18x Redis’s, and pipelined throughput improved from around 60k requests/sec to 300k+, once pipelined commands were batched into a single dispatch round trip instead of paying a channel handoff per command.

There’s still a real, measurable gap on the non-pipelined path, and it’s worth being precise about where that’s likely coming from rather than assuming.

4.1 What profiling actually showed

Here’s the CPU breakdown from an earlier profiling run (go tool pprof, ~20 seconds sampled under sustained redis-benchmark load), by line — I don’t have the raw trace files anymore, but the numbers are from that run:

Cost % of total CPU Cause
writer.Flush() 37.6% The TCP write syscall for each reply — largely inherent to non-pipelined request/response
core.Decode() 19.3% RESP parsing off the socket
dispatchWorker command dispatch 6.4% Actual command execution (store lookup, RESP encode)
Channel send/recv/alloc (replych, commandCh) ~4.7% The cost of handing each command off to the single dispatch worker via a channel

Two things stand out. First, the single biggest cost (writer.Flush()) is largely inherent to a non-pipelined request/response protocol in general — every command needs its own network round trip, and Redis pays a version of this cost too, just without a userspace scheduler involved. Second, the channel-handoff cost, while real, was the smallest line item in that particular run — smaller than logging and deadline-polling overhead were before those got fixed. That’s a useful reminder: it’s easy to reason your way to “the channel design must be the bottleneck” from first principles (Go’s goroutine park/wake is genuinely more expensive than a C event loop’s inline execution), and that reasoning is sound, but the actual weight of that cost in the total budget is something only a fresh profile can confirm — not intuition.

TipWhy real Redis doesn’t pay the channel cost

Redis is also single-threaded for command execution — one command at a time, same as rediska’s one-worker model. But it runs inside a plain C event loop calling epoll_wait, with no second thread to hand a command off to. Rediska’s design adds a cross-goroutine hop through a channel for every command, which the Go runtime implements via a goroutine park/wake cycle — real overhead, even if the profile above shows it isn’t currently the dominant one.

5 What’s Left to Test

A few things would sharpen this picture rather than leave it at “roughly 1.18x slower”:

  1. Re-profile on current code. The breakdown above predates some of the later fixes; a fresh pprof run under the same redis-benchmark load would show whether the channel-handoff share has grown relative to Flush/Decode now that logging and deadline overhead are gone.
  2. Try a mutex-guarded direct-dispatch path as an experiment, comparing it against the current channel design under identical load, to get a real before/after number rather than an estimate.
  3. Benchmark a wider command set. Current numbers are mostly SET/GET/INCR; transactions, HyperLogLog, and pipelined batches with mixed command types haven’t been benchmarked in isolation yet.
  4. Test under memory pressure. Exercise the LRU/LFU eviction paths under a constrained maxmemory with realistic access patterns, not just correctness tests, to see how eviction sampling overhead behaves under load.
  5. Test AOF durability under load and crash. Recovery correctness has been checked; recovery time and AOF write overhead under sustained write-heavy load haven’t been measured.
  6. Scale concurrent clients further. Current benchmarks use a fixed concurrency level; sweeping connection counts would show whether the gap to Redis widens, narrows, or stays flat as concurrency increases.

6 Appendix: Repository

Code referenced in this post is from vinayhpandya/learning-redis.

item.title: Building and Evaluating a Search Engine Over Malware-Classification Papers
item.dc:creator: Vinay Pandya
item.description:
Overview

This project builds a search engine over a corpus of arXiv malware-classification papers, implementing and comparing seven retrieval methods head-to-head: BM25 → dense (SPECTER2) → hybrid (RRF) → cross-encoder rerank → late-interaction (ColBERT via Qdrant) → k-means cluster-filtered search → generative retrieval (a trained query→semantic-ID model).

Every method is evaluated on the same 40-query, LLM-judged relevance-labeled eval set, using the same NDCG@10 / MRR metrics, and benchmarked on the same latency harness. The goal was not just to build each technique, but to honestly report where each one wins, where it loses, and why — including findings that didn’t come out the way theory alone would predict.

Code: github.com/vinayhpandya/search-algorithms

Corpus and Setup

  • Domain: arXiv papers on malware classification (cs.CR, cs.LG, cs.CV categories), collected via the arxiv client library across 16 search queries, deduplicated
  • Enrichment: citation counts from Semantic Scholar (used later as an LTR feature)
  • Index: OpenSearch, single-node local Docker setup — chosen because it supports BM25 and k-NN vector search natively in one engine, letting lexical and semantic search share the same index and fuse without cross-system round trips
  • Scope decision: abstract-only (no full-text PDFs), to keep the repo small and the project achievable in a weekend — noted as future work

Methodology: Evaluation

Relevance labeling

Manually labeling enough query-paper pairs for a meaningful eval set (857+ pairs across 40 queries) isn’t realistic by hand in the available time. Instead:

  1. A researcher LLM rates each pair 0/1/2 with a rationale
  2. A critic LLM reviews the researcher’s rating and either confirms or overrides it — final label = critic’s call
  3. A human spot-check on a stratified sample (~65 pairs, weighted toward researcher/critic disagreements) validates the LLM labels

This is standard practice for evaluating relevance judgments at scale (the same logic behind TREC-style IR evaluation and industry search-quality teams checking LLM/crowd-worker judgments) — not a shortcut.

Known calibration issue: only ~3% of labeled pairs were rated “not relevant” (0). Because candidate pools are built from real search results (already topically adjacent to the query), the researcher/critic prompts turned out lenient about what counts as irrelevant. This doesn’t invalidate the labels — NDCG@10 still discriminates well since it weights label=2 three times as heavily as label=1 — but it does mean MRR at the standard threshold (label ≥ 1) saturates near 1.0 for every method and carries no signal. Reporting MRR at threshold ≥ 2 (“how often is the very best result found immediately”) restored real discrimination between methods without needing to relabel anything. (A tighter, binary relevance rubric was designed as a follow-up fix but not run before this writeup — noted under Future Work.)

Metrics

  • NDCG@10: rewards ranking highly-relevant results near the top; uses the full graded (0/1/2) label
  • MRR(≥2): reciprocal rank of the first highly relevant result — the metric that actually discriminates given this corpus’s label distribution
  • Latency: mean / p50 / p95 across 40 queries, local machine, no GPU

Results: Retrieval Quality

Method NDCG@10 MRR(≥1) MRR(≥2)
BM25 0.9003 1.0000 0.5969
Dense 0.9026 1.0000 0.5763
Hybrid 0.9142 1.0000 0.7261
Rerank 0.9131 1.0000 0.7504
Late-interaction 0.9003 1.0000 0.6951
Semantic ID (k-means, cluster-filtered) 0.9624 0.9625 0.2744
Generative (RQ-VAE + trained query→ID model) 0.9005 1.0000 0.2432

Reading the core four methods

Dense underperforms BM25 on MRR(≥2) (0.5763 vs 0.5969) despite near-identical NDCG@10 — SPECTER2 embeddings surface broadly topical neighbors well, but are less precise than exact keyword matching at pinpointing the single best match at rank 1.

Hybrid and rerank both correct for this, each clearly outperforming either input alone on MRR(≥2) — real evidence of fusion and reranking doing genuine work, not just reshuffling noise.

Late-interaction lands between dense and hybrid (MRR≥2 = 0.6951) — consistent with the theoretical expectation that token-level (MaxSim) matching captures finer-grained relevance than single-vector cosine similarity, without needing full cross-attention.

Rerank is the best quality by both metrics — expected, since a cross-encoder sees the full query and document jointly via cross-attention (strictly more expressive than any similarity-metric-based method here), at the cost of only being feasible on a pre-filtered shortlist, never the whole corpus.

Two different semantic-ID-based methods, two different stories

Both remaining rows use “semantic IDs” but are otherwise unrelated methods, worth not conflating:

  • Semantic ID (k-means): a two-level k-means clustering over SPECTER2 embeddings, used to pre-filter/organize the corpus (IVF-style). Highest NDCG@10 of all seven methods (0.9624) but by far the lowest MRR(≥2) (0.2744) — it reliably finds something topically adjacent, but rarely the single best paper. A fixed, non-learned clustering, not a retrieval model in its own right.
  • Generative retrieval: a genuinely trained model (RQ-VAE + query→ID decoder, detailed below) that predicts a semantic ID directly from the query text and looks up matching papers — the actual “generative retrieval” paradigm this project set out to test.

Generative Retrieval: What Was Actually Built

Beyond the six baseline methods above, a from-scratch generative retrieval pipeline was implemented, following the two-stage design used in TIGER-style semantic ID systems:

Stage 1 — RQ-VAE. A small encoder/decoder (MLP, 768→512→256→32) with a 2-level residual vector quantizer (16 codewords/level, EMA codebook updates, dead-code reset) trained on SPECTER2 embeddings to produce a hierarchical 2-digit semantic ID per paper ([coarse, fine]). Trained on the full 194-paper corpus; qualitative inspection showed genuinely topic-coherent clusters (e.g. one cluster grouped five adversarial-malware-attack papers, another grouped five malware-classification-methods papers).

Stage 2 — query-to-ID model. Since no real user queries exist, ~1,940 synthetic (query, semantic_id) pairs were generated via LLM (10 queries per paper, mixing keyword-close and oblique natural-language phrasings). A frozen MiniLM sentence encoder + small 2-layer transformer decoder was trained to autoregressively predict a paper’s semantic ID digit-by-digit from a query, with beam search at inference time. Train/val split was done by paper, not by row, to prevent different phrasings of the same paper’s queries leaking across the split.

Evaluation methodology. The trained model was wired into the same eval harness as the other six methods: for each of the 40 eval queries, beam search produces ranked candidate semantic IDs, each ID’s matching papers are pulled in beam order to build a ranked top-10 list, and that list is scored with the same NDCG@10/MRR machinery and LLM-judged labels used throughout.

Result: a clear, honest negative finding. Training showed a real generalization gap — training exact-match accuracy climbed to 36% while validation exact-match stayed near 2–5%, i.e. the model was memorizing training-set query phrasings rather than learning to generalize across topics. This is directly reflected in the eval numbers: NDCG@10 (0.9005) looks reasonable only because the label set skews lenient (see calibration note above), while MRR(≥2) (0.2432) — the metric that actually measures whether the single best paper is found — is among the weakest of all seven methods. The most likely cause, and the most actionable finding: 194 papers (165 after the train/val split) is simply too little topic diversity for a 256-way discrete prediction task to generalize from — an architecture problem this isn’t; a data-scale problem it is. Scaling to a larger corpus (e.g. the ~100k-paper ML-ArXiv-Papers subset) is the natural next step to test that hypothesis directly.

Latency

Mean / p50 / p95 across 40 queries, local machine, no GPU:

Method Mean (ms) P50 (ms) P95 (ms)
BM25 2.7 2.6 3.3
Late-interaction 12.6 12.3 16.0
Generative 20.4 20.0 23.9
Semantic ID (k-means) 30.5 30.4 36.0
Dense 42.7 42.7 48.0
Hybrid 59.6 59.4 64.8
Rerank 187.8 186.8 200.9

BM25 is fastest by a wide margin, as expected — no model inference at all. Generative retrieval lands in the middle of the pack: slower than BM25 and late-interaction, but notably faster than dense search despite also requiring a forward pass, since the query encoder here (frozen MiniLM) is far smaller than SPECTER2, and lookup after ID prediction is a cheap dictionary access rather than a k-NN search over the full corpus. Rerank is the clear latency outlier, consistent with cross-encoders’ cost scaling with the number of candidates scored, not just query size — the tradeoff that pairs it with a cheap first-stage retriever in practice rather than running it corpus-wide.

Future Work

  • Rerun evaluation under a binary (0/1), query-specific relevance rubric — designed to fix the labeling calibration issue described above, but not executed before this writeup.
  • Scale the corpus (e.g. to the ~100k-paper ML-ArXiv-Papers subset) to directly test whether generative retrieval’s weak MRR(≥2) is a data-scale problem, as the evidence here suggests, rather than an architectural one.
  • Hypencoders Testing a small Qnet and hype-encoder based network, want to see how fast it is to train and how well the NDCG scores are
  • Full-text PDFs and a RAG QA layer on top of the retrieval stack — scoped out from the very beginning to keep this project achievable in the available time.

item.title: Building a Production-Grade LLM Inference Stack: Benchmarking vLLM, Ray Serve, and MoE Models
item.dc:creator: Vinay Pandya
Yiran Xu
item.description:
1 Introduction

These are our notes from benchmarking a self-hosted LLM inference stack. The goal was practical: figure out which combination of model, serving framework, and infrastructure actually holds up under realistic load, and where the real trade-offs are.

I tested four configurations:

  • Qwen2.5-7B on Ray Serve + vLLM (production baseline)
  • DeepSeek-V2-Lite MoE with disaggregated prefill
  • DeepSeek-V2-Lite MoE without disaggregated prefill
  • LLaMA 3.1-8B with LMCache on Modal (serverless)

The finding that surprised me most: the same DeepSeek model showed a 13x throughput difference depending solely on whether disaggregated prefill was enabled. That’s not a model choice — it’s a configuration choice, and it’s easy to get wrong.

2 Architecture Overview

2.1 The Full Stack

Layer Responsibilities:

Layer Technology Purpose
Load Balancer Nginx SSE streaming, long timeouts for cold starts
Agent Layer LangGraph ReAct loop with tool calling (web search, calculator)
API Gateway FastAPI Request routing, backend selection, metrics
Inference vLLM + Ray Serve High-throughput model serving
Monitoring Prometheus + Grafana Real-time metrics and alerting

2.2 Why This Architecture?

A few decisions worth noting. Nginx sits at the front because SSE streaming requires careful timeout handling that most default configs don’t cover. The FastAPI gateway makes it straightforward to swap inference backends without changing anything on the client side. And running Prometheus from the start, even during experiments, meant I could catch degradation as it happened rather than reconstructing it from logs.

3 Experiment Methodology

3.1 Testing Phases

All experiments use the ShareGPT dataset:

4.3 Key Findings

NoteQwen2.5-7B Performance Summary
  • 100% success rate across all concurrency levels (1–16)
  • TTFT p50: 408–564ms, stable across load levels
  • Throughput: 34–37 tokens/sec, essentially flat
  • Latency increases linearly with concurrency — no sudden cliff

Qwen held up well. What I didn’t expect was how flat the throughput curve stayed — it didn’t gain much as concurrency increased, but it also didn’t degrade. The linear latency scaling makes it straightforward to set SLAs: if p50 is 408ms at concurrency 1, you can roughly estimate what it’ll look like at higher load without surprises.

Its tool-calling reliability is also notably good, which matters for the agent layer. This is why it’s the production baseline.

5 Experiment 2: DeepSeek MoE with Disaggregated Prefill

5.1 What is Disaggregated Prefill?

LLM inference has two distinct phases:

  1. Prefill: Process input tokens (compute-bound)
  2. Decode: Generate output tokens one at a time (memory-bound)

These phases have very different resource profiles. Disaggregated prefill separates them onto different workers so each can be tuned independently. For MoE models, this matters more than usual — expert routing during prefill adds overhead that gets in the way of efficient decoding if both phases share the same worker.

5.2 Setup

  • Model: DeepSeek-V2-Lite-Chat (16B total, 2.4B active parameters)
  • Framework: Ray Serve + vLLM with PD disaggregation
  • Infrastructure: Anyscale (g5.12xlarge, 4x A10G)

5.4 Key Findings

ImportantDeepSeek Disaggregated Performance
  • 85 tokens/sec at concurrency=1 — 2.3x higher than Qwen
  • 100% success rate across all load levels
  • TTFT p50: 406ms, on par with Qwen despite a much larger model
  • MoE efficiency only materializes with the right infrastructure

The throughput number was the clearest result from the whole experiment. 85 tokens/sec from a 16B-parameter model, with TTFT matching a 7B model, is only possible because the disaggregated setup lets the prefill and decode workers each do what they’re actually good at. Without it, the picture is very different — see the next section.

6 Experiment 3: DeepSeek WITHOUT Disaggregation

I ran the same DeepSeek model without disaggregated prefill to make the comparison concrete.

6.1 Results

This is the same model, same hardware, different configuration. The 13x throughput gap isn’t about the model — it’s about whether the serving infrastructure matches how MoE models actually work. Picking a MoE model without accounting for this will result in significantly worse performance than a smaller dense model.

7 Experiment 4: LLaMA 3.1-8B with LMCache on Modal

7.1 Setup

  • Model: LLaMA 3.1-8B with LMCache (prefix caching)
  • Framework: vLLM on Modal (serverless)
  • Optimization: Prefix caching for repeated prompts

7.2 Results

LLaMA 3.1-8B with LMCache on Modal

7.3 Key Findings

Modal’s serverless deployment caps out around 4 concurrent requests, with throughput between 25–26 tokens/sec. It starts failing above 1.0 RPS on sustained load. The cold start penalty is real, and it shows up in the TTFT numbers under anything resembling steady traffic.

That said, scale-to-zero is a meaningful cost advantage if your workload is bursty. For development, testing, or low-traffic use cases where you’re not running requests continuously, you won’t pay for idle GPU time. That trade-off just doesn’t work for anything that needs consistent throughput.

7.4 Trade-offs

Pros Cons
Scale-to-zero (cost savings) Cold start latency
Simple deployment Lower throughput ceiling
Good for bursty workloads Not suitable for sustained load

9 Recommendations

9.1 Decision Matrix

9.2 When to Use What

  1. Production APIs with tool-calling: Qwen2.5-7B on Ray Serve
    • Highest reliability (100% success)
    • Excellent function-calling support
    • Predictable latency for SLAs
  2. Maximum throughput batch processing: DeepSeek with disaggregated prefill
    • 2.3x faster than alternatives
    • Cost-efficient for high-volume workloads
  3. Cost-sensitive, bursty workloads: Modal + LMCache
    • Scale-to-zero saves money during idle periods
    • Good for development and testing
  4. Avoid: Non-disaggregated MoE deployments
    • 13x throughput penalty is rarely acceptable

10 Lessons Learned

NoteKey Takeaways

  1. Infrastructure configuration can outweigh model selection. The DeepSeek results make this point clearly — a misconfigured 16B model underperformed a well-configured 7B model on every metric.

  2. MoE models require disaggregated prefill to reach their potential. Without it, the prefill and decode phases compete for the same resources, and you end up with the worst of both.

  3. Single-request benchmarks are not enough. The concurrency sweep and sustained RPS phases revealed limits that didn’t show up at low load.

  4. TTFT and total latency tell different stories. A model can have acceptable total latency but poor TTFT, which matters a lot for interactive use cases where users are waiting for the stream to start.

  5. Serverless is a cost tool, not a performance tool. Modal is useful when GPU utilization would otherwise be near zero. It’s not a substitute for a properly configured persistent cluster under real load.

11 Conclusions

If I had to distill this down: for a production API with tool-calling requirements, Qwen2.5-7B on Ray Serve is the most reliable option based on these experiments. If throughput is the priority and you’re willing to configure it correctly, DeepSeek with disaggregated prefill is clearly the better choice. The serverless option on Modal works for specific cost scenarios but has real ceiling constraints that rule it out for sustained workloads.

The most important thing these experiments confirmed is that getting the infrastructure right matters as much as picking the right model. The difference between a well-configured and a poorly-configured MoE deployment is not marginal — it’s the difference between a useful system and one that fails a third of its requests.
